title: 1-D DP
summary: In 1-D DP the state is a single index: the best answer for a prefix, or for a run that ends at position i. Each cell reads a few earlier cells, or every earlier cell when any of them could come just before.
idea: dp[i] = answer for the prefix up to i (or ending at i). Build it from earlier cells; the answer is dp[n] or the best dp[i].

signals.see: A sequence, string or number line, and the answer for position i depends only on earlier positions.
signals.think: One index is enough state. Ask: what is the last step into position i, and where could it come from?

signals.see: 'Longest increasing…', 'number of ways to decode or split…', 'can the string be broken into words…'.
signals.think: Each of these looks back at some or all earlier cells: dp[i] combines dp[j] for valid j < i.

signals.see: The recurrence only reads the last one or two cells.
signals.think: Keep two variables instead of the whole array to get O(1) space.

phrasings: Find the length of the longest strictly rising subsequence.
Count the ways to turn a string of digits back into letters, where 1 is A and 26 is Z.
Can this sentence without spaces be split into dictionary words?

picture.title: Trying every subsequence versus a best run ending at each index
picture.alt: On the left, every subsequence is listed and checked, which is 2 to the n options. On the right, dp[i] stores the longest rising run that ends at index i; it is found by looking back at every smaller earlier value j and adding one to dp[j].
picture.caption: Store the best answer that ends at each index, then look back.

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 8 whole numbers from −99 to 99.

oneLiner: dp[i] = best ending at i = combine dp[j] for valid j < i; answer = dp[n] or max(dp)

exercise.prompt: A message of letters was encoded as digits, with A = 1 up to Z = 26, and the spaces were lost. Given the digit string s, return how many different messages it could have been. A 0 can only be the second digit of 10 or 20. The starter decodes a lone 0 as a letter.
hints: dp[i] is the number of ways to decode the first i digits. dp[0] = 1: the empty prefix decodes one way.
The last letter used either one digit (it must not be 0) or two digits (they must form 10 to 26).
Add dp[i − 1] for the one-digit case and dp[i − 2] for the two-digit case.

complexity.time: O(n²); O(n) for a fixed reach
complexity.why: Looking back at every earlier index costs O(n) per cell. When dp[i] reads only dp[i − 1] and dp[i − 2], each cell is O(1) and two variables replace the array.

mistakes: Returning dp[n − 1] when the best run can end anywhere, so the answer is max(dp).
Using ≤ instead of < when the question says strictly increasing.
Setting dp[0] = 0 in counting problems, when the empty prefix has exactly one way.
Forgetting that a digit or word can fail to match, so some dp cells stay 0.

quiz.question: For the longest rising subsequence, why is the answer max(dp) and not dp[n − 1]?
choices: dp[i] is the best run that ends at i, and the best run may end earlier
quiz.explain: The state is 'ends at i', so every cell is a candidate answer.

quiz.question: In stair climbing with steps of 1 or 2, how much memory do you really need?
choices: Two variables: the last two values
quiz.explain: dp[i] reads only dp[i − 1] and dp[i − 2], so keep a rolling pair.

quiz.question: For decoding digits, what is dp[0]?
choices: 1: there is one way to decode nothing
quiz.explain: Counting DP usually starts from 1 way for the empty case, so the first real choice has something to build on.

interviewTip: Say whether your state means 'using the first i items' or 'ending at index i'. The difference decides the answer cell and catches most off-by-one bugs.
